assessment.name: Year 8 History Autumn assessment
assessment.sections: In your first History lesson in the week of 30 November, in class (50 minutes).
assessment.weighting: Topic list: Story summary: The Oba of Benin. How can we tell the story of Nur Jahan? Did the Puritans transform England?

mock.note: 30 questions from the revision lesson topics. Then answer one written question from the Written practice tab.

units.name: Nur Jahan and the Mughal Empire
How historians tell Nur Jahan's story
Puritans, Elizabeth I and James I
Charles I and the Civil War
The Republic: did the Puritans transform England?

cards.title: Benin City and the power of the Oba
cards.question: How did the Oba of Benin show his power?
points: Benin's capital was Benin City, protected by enormous walls and guarded gates.
The ruler was called the Oba. He appeared in public only once a year, which made him seem special and powerful.
His vast royal palace was like a city within a city, with a huge brass snake on the roof and brass birds on pillars.

Craftspeople made bronze plaques of kings and queens. People believed the plaques gained spiritual power in the palace. A legend said an Oba defeated the sea god, giving the Obas power over the ocean.
cards.watch_out: The plaques were made of bronze (and brass), not gold. They recorded Benin's history and celebrated its rulers.
cards.hook: Walls, palace, plaques: three ways the Oba projected power.
cards.grade9: Explain why being rarely seen made the Oba more powerful: mystery made people respect him as almost divine.

cards.title: Ruling Benin: the Iyoba and the nobles
cards.question: Who helped the Oba to rule Benin?
points: The queen mother, called the Iyoba, used her knowledge of spells and magic to help keep the Oba on the throne.
A council of nobles helped the Oba make decisions on war, trade and taxes.
Nobles were rich and powerful: one rode past on a decorated horse with servants holding sunshades.
Markets sold leopard skins, fine cloth, gold dust, ivory, yams, fish, pepper and red coral (used to decorate nobles' clothes).
cards.watch_out: The Iyoba was the Oba's mother, not his wife.
cards.grade9: Compare the Oba with Mansa Musa of Mali: both used wealth and display to project power.

cards.title: Benin and Portugal
cards.question: What connections did Benin have with Portugal, and how did trade change?
points: Portuguese merchants came by sea, eager for Benin's riches. They brought guns, cloth and coral.
At first they wanted ivory and pepper. Later they wanted Benin cloth.
The Oba refused to let the Portuguese convert Benin to Christianity, because it would weaken his religious authority.
The cloth trade weakened the Oba because cloth was sold straight to Portuguese merchants without his involvement.
Benin nobles bought enslaved people (prisoners of war from neighbouring kingdoms) to sell to the Portuguese.
cards.watch_out: The traders came from Portugal, not Spain or England.
cards.hook: Ivory and pepper, then cloth, then people: how the Portuguese trade changed.
cards.grade9: Explain the link between trade and power: when trade went around the Oba, he lost control of wealth and influence.

cards.title: Mihr's early life and the Mughal Empire
cards.question: Who was Mihr, and why did her family move to India?
points: Mihr was born in 1577 while her family travelled from Persia to India along the Silk Road.
The Mughal Empire ruled much of India. Its emperors were Muslim, though most Indians were Hindu.
Her father joined the court of Emperor Akbar as an adviser. The family sought wealth and peace.
In 1594 Mihr married a Mughal government officer in Bengal. He was killed in 1607 after being linked to a rebellion against the new emperor, Jahangir.
cards.watch_out: Akbar was the emperor when Mihr arrived. Jahangir, his son, became emperor in 1605.
cards.hook: Akbar first, then Jahangir, then Shah Jahan: A, J, S.
cards.grade9: Explain why the Silk Road mattered: it connected the Mughal Empire to Persia and beyond, bringing trade, ideas and people.

cards.title: Becoming Nur Jahan
cards.question: How did Mihr become Nur Jahan, and how did she use her new status?
points: After her husband's death she lived in Jahangir's harem in Agra. She met Jahangir in the palace bazaar.
In 1611 she married Emperor Jahangir, becoming his twentieth wife.
She cared for Jahangir, gave gifts to the poor and arranged marriages for 500 orphan girls.
In 1617 Jahangir named her Nur Jahan, meaning Light of the World.
cards.watch_out: She became his favourite wife because of her kindness and ability, not only because of the marriage.
cards.grade9: Show how her actions built trust and support, which she later used to rule.

cards.title: The Camp of Good Fortune and the tiger hunt
cards.question: What was the Camp of Good Fortune, and how did Nur Jahan impress people?
points: The Camp of Good Fortune was the portable royal city of tents that moved with Jahangir's court. About 100 000 people travelled with it.
Nur held audiences in her own tent and won the support of powerful noblemen by giving gifts: clothing, diamonds, elephants and gold.
She worked to stop Jahangir's sons from plotting rebellions.
In 1617, riding an elephant, she killed four tigers with just six shots.
cards.watch_out: Four tigers, six shots. Learn the numbers exactly.
cards.grade9: Explain why the court moved: to keep watch on officials and army leaders, and to show the emperor's power across the empire.

cards.title: Nur Jahan takes control
cards.question: How did Nur Jahan rule the empire and rescue Jahangir?
points: Jahangir drank too much wine and became addicted to opium, so Nur ruled the government during his illnesses.
She decided on land for nobles, taxes and criminal cases, and had coins made with her own name.
She designed a white marble tomb for her parents in Agra. Its design inspired the Taj Mahal.
In 1626 General Mahabat kidnapped Jahangir. Nur led loyal soldiers on an elephant across a river to rescue him.
cards.watch_out: Nur did not build the Taj Mahal. Shah Jahan built it later, using white marble like Nur's tomb design.
cards.grade9: Use the rescue as evidence of her military leadership, which was very unusual for a Mughal woman.

cards.title: After Jahangir
cards.question: What happened to Nur Jahan after Jahangir died?
points: Jahangir died in 1627.
Shah Jahan, Jahangir's third son, became emperor.
Nur Jahan went to live in Lahore.
She continued to design buildings and gardens until her death in 1645.
cards.watch_out: Shah Jahan was Jahangir's son, not Nur Jahan's son.
cards.grade9: Judge her legacy: she shaped Mughal architecture and showed a woman could share imperial power.

cards.title: How historians found Nur Jahan's story
cards.question: Which sources did the historian Ruby Lal use to tell Nur Jahan's story?
points: Some historians laughed and said there were no sources about Mughal women. Ruby Lal searched the court records.
Written orders: ten survive. They show Nur made decisions about taxes, land, the army and criminal cases, like the emperor.
The Jahangirnama: Jahangir's diary, which mentions Nur more than thirty times, including the tiger hunt.
Coins with her name show she wanted to project her power. Paintings show her in action, such as loading a musket.
cards.watch_out: The Jahangirnama was written by Jahangir himself (and later a nobleman), so it may praise Nur because he loved her.
cards.grade9: Decide which source tells us most: written orders prove real power, while the diary may be biased.

cards.title: Who were the Puritans?
cards.question: Who were the Puritans and what did they believe?
points: Puritans were Protestant Christians who believed the English Reformation had not gone far enough.
They wanted to purify the church of anything that looked Catholic, such as vestments (special robes for priests), images and praying to saints.
They told people to avoid working on Sunday, swearing and drunkenness, to obey God's laws.
Ten years into Elizabeth I's reign they were frustrated because people still worshipped images and prayed to saints.
cards.watch_out: Puritans were Protestants, not Catholics. They disliked anything that reminded them of Catholicism.
cards.grade9: Explain why Puritans disliked bishops: bishops reminded them of the Catholic Church and punished Puritans for not worshipping as the king commanded.

cards.title: King James I
cards.question: What happened when James became king, and how did Puritans react?
points: After Elizabeth I died in 1603, King James became king of England, Scotland and Ireland.
Catholics hoped for change because his mother, Mary Queen of Scots, was Catholic, but James was Protestant.
In 1605 Guy Fawkes and other Catholics plotted to murder James (the Gunpowder Plot).
James threw expensive feasts to win the nobles' loyalty. When he asked Parliament (Lords and Commons) for new taxes, they said no.
Puritan town leaders arrested drunkards, expelled theatre groups and banned dancing on Sundays. From 1620 many Puritans migrated to North America.
cards.watch_out: Parliament had two chambers: the House of Lords and the House of Commons.
cards.grade9: Show change and continuity: Puritans changed some towns, but could not change the whole country under James.

cards.title: Charles I and his conflict with Parliament
cards.question: Why did Charles I fall out with Parliament and the Puritans?
points: Charles I became king when James died. He married the French Catholic princess Henrietta Maria for money and soldiers.
He raised £250 000 without Parliament's permission in the first years of his reign.
When Puritans in the Commons accused him of spreading popery (Catholic ways) and demanded the abolition of bishops, he dissolved Parliament and ruled without it for 11 years.
Archbishop William Laud and the bishops controlled the Church of England. Many Puritan protesters were imprisoned and had their ears cut off.
cards.watch_out: Henrietta Maria was Catholic, which made Puritans more suspicious of Charles.
cards.grade9: Link causes together: money, religion and power all pushed king and Parliament apart.

cards.title: The road to civil war
cards.question: How did the conflict between Charles I and Parliament lead to war?
points: Charles tried to control the Scottish church with a new prayer book. The Scots (the Covenanters) rebelled.
In 1640 Charles recalled Parliament because he needed money to fight the Scots.
The 1640 Parliament was dominated by Puritans.
By 1642 England was in civil war between the king (Royalists) and Parliament. The Puritan Oliver Cromwell became a brilliant general.
cards.watch_out: Charles recalled Parliament because he needed money, not because he wanted to share power.
cards.grade9: Explain why Cromwell thought he won: he believed God had chosen him to defeat the king.

cards.title: The execution of the king and the Republic
cards.question: What happened after Parliament won the Civil War?
points: During the war the Puritans abolished bishops and banned Christmas celebrations.
King Charles I was executed in January 1649.
England became a republic: a country ruled without a monarch.
Cromwell later became Lord Protector and placed England under the control of his generals.
In the 1650s Puritan soldiers shut down drinking houses and theatres.
cards.watch_out: Executing a king was shocking. Even many Parliament supporters did not want it.
cards.grade9: Explain why the Puritans were so strict: they wanted to make England a godly country and believed sin would bring God's punishment.

cards.title: Did the Puritans transform England?
cards.question: How would you answer the question Did the Puritans transform England?
points: Yes: the king was executed, bishops were abolished, Christmas was banned, theatres and drinking houses were closed.
No: many people secretly kept celebrating Christmas, for example roasting apples and baking Christmas pies.
No: after Cromwell died in 1658, the monarchy was restored in 1660 with King Charles II.
Judgement: the Puritans changed England for a time, but most changes did not last.
cards.watch_out: A strong answer gives both sides and then a clear judgement, not just a list of events.
cards.hook: Changed for a while, not for ever.
cards.grade9: Use the words short term and long term in your judgement to show depth.

cards.title: Key dates and names
cards.question: Can you put these key dates and people in order?
points: Benin: the Oba, the Iyoba, council of nobles, Portugal.
1577 Mihr born; 1605 Jahangir emperor; 1611 marries Jahangir; 1617 named Nur Jahan, tiger hunt; 1626 rescue; 1627 Jahangir dies; 1645 Nur dies.
1603 James I; 1605 Gunpowder Plot; 1620 Puritans to North America.
Charles I: 11 years without Parliament; 1640 recalls Parliament; 1642 civil war; 1649 executed.
Republic in the 1650s; Cromwell Lord Protector; 1660 monarchy restored.
cards.watch_out: Use dates in your written answers. They show precise knowledge.

written.q: Explain how the Oba of Benin projected his power.
model: Benin City was protected by enormous walls and gates (1)
His huge palace, like a city within a city, with brass snakes and birds, showed wealth (1)
He appeared in public only once a year, making him seem special (1)
Bronze plaques celebrated rulers and were believed to gain spiritual power (1)
He refused to let the Portuguese spread Christianity, protecting his religious authority (1)
Explanation linking these to how people saw the Oba as powerful (1)

written.q: How did Nur Jahan help to rule the Mughal Empire? Use at least three examples.
model: She gave gifts to noblemen at the Camp of Good Fortune to win loyalty (1)
She worked to stop Jahangir's sons from rebelling (1)
She ruled during Jahangir's illness: taxes, land and criminal cases (1)
She had coins made in her own name (1)
She led the rescue of Jahangir from General Mahabat in 1626 (1)
Explanation of why this was unusual for a Mughal woman (1)

written.q: Which source tells historians the most about Nur Jahan? Explain your answer.
model: Names a source, such as her written orders (1)
Explains what it shows, such as decisions on taxes and land (1)
Compares with another source, such as the Jahangirnama, which may be biased (1)
Reaches a judgement with a reason (1)

written.q: Did the Puritans transform England? Explain your answer.
model: Change: Charles I executed in 1649 and England became a republic (1)
Change: bishops abolished and Christmas banned (1)
Change: theatres and drinking houses closed by Puritan soldiers (1)
Continuity: many people secretly celebrated Christmas (1)
Continuity: the monarchy was restored in 1660 (1)
Uses dates and specific detail throughout (1)
Clear judgement, for example changed in the short term but not the long term (2)

exam_tips.timing: 50 minutes. Spend about 1 minute per mark, and save 10 minutes for the longest written question.
section_a: Learn the key dates for Nur Jahan and the Puritans.
section_b: Use specific details, names and dates as evidence.
For a big question like Did the Puritans transform England, give both sides then a judgement.
Explain why each point matters, not just what happened.

vocab.meaning: To show an image of yourself, such as power, to others
vocab.example: The Oba used bronze plaques to project his power.

vocab.meaning: A person who buys and sells goods
vocab.example: A Portuguese merchant came to Benin to buy pepper.

vocab.meaning: A group of lands ruled by one ruler
vocab.example: The Mughal Empire ruled much of India.

vocab.meaning: A friendly agreement between people or groups to support each other
vocab.example: Nur Jahan built an alliance with powerful noblemen.

vocab.meaning: Something from the past that tells us about it
vocab.example: The Jahangirnama is an important source about Nur Jahan.

vocab.meaning: A Protestant who wanted to purify the church of Catholic practices
vocab.example: A Puritan would avoid working on Sunday.

vocab.meaning: The group that makes laws, with the House of Lords and the House of Commons
vocab.example: Parliament refused to give King James new taxes.

vocab.meaning: A country ruled without a king or queen
vocab.example: England became a republic after Charles I was executed.

vocab.meaning: Killing someone as a legal punishment
vocab.example: The execution of Charles I shocked many people.
The Puritans tried to transform England into a godly country.
